issues.issue: The covenant is conditioned on "the enactment of concurrent legislation ... having the same effect as this Part," yet the federal enacting statute in Part II (Section 15.1 Reservations) attaches conditions that vary the compact's terms. A court could be asked whether legislation containing such reservations is legislation "having the same effect," and what the covenant binds the parties to.

Section 1.1 names "this Act" the Delaware River Basin Compact, while Section 1.2(c) defines "Compact" as Part I of the act only. The two provisions give the same word different reach, so it is unclear whether Part II (the reservations and state effectuation sections) is part of the Compact.

"Area of drainage into the Delaware River and its tributaries" fixes no boundary for ground water or for land whose surface drainage is diverted, so the geographic reach of "Basin" is indeterminate. Because Section 2.7 limits the commission's powers to "the limits of the basin," the vagueness is jurisdictional.

Defining "Compact" as Part I only leaves the Part II federal reservations (Section 15.1) outside the defined term, although they expressly override compact sections such as 2.2, 3.7 and 11.5. A court could be asked whether provisions saying "nothing contained in the Compact" reach those reservations at all.

"Net induced adverse effects, whether or not compensated for" is a cost component with no method or boundary of measurement stated. The term drives assessments under Section 4.3 and cost allocations under Section 11.4, so its indeterminacy is operative.

"Facility" is defined by an open catch-all — "any and all things and appurtenances necessary, useful or convenient" — appended to a list of water-related structures, raising an ejusdem generis question about how far beyond water works it reaches. Whether privately owned industrial works such as well pads are "facilities" acquired or operated "for the beneficial use of water resources" is genuinely contestable.

"Any appropriate branch, department, bureau or division thereof, as the case may be" supplies no criterion of appropriateness, so which federal entity is bound as the "Federal government" in a given section is left open.

"Project" — "any work, service or activity which is separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission, or any separate facility undertaken ... for the conservation, utilization, control, development or management of water resources" — is syntactically ambiguous as to whether "by the commission" qualifies the whole clause and whether privately undertaken industrial activity such as a gas well falls within it. The qualifying phrases "which can be established and utilized independently" and "considered as a separate entity for purposes of evaluation" give no workable boundary.

Read with Section 3.8, which subjects projects "undertaken by any person, corporation or governmental authority" to commission approval, the definition's reference to planning, financing or identification "by the commission" cannot easily be squared with the referral-and-review regime. A court must decide whether 3.8 reaches activities the commission never planned, financed or identified.

"Water resources" is defined to "include" water and "related natural resources in, on, under, or above the ground, including related uses of land" — an inclusive, unbounded formula with no test of relatedness. Whether subsurface minerals such as natural gas, or the land uses that extract them, are "related natural resources" is the contestable point.

This is a legislative finding, not an operative grant, yet it declares the management of basin water resources to be "public purposes" in terms broad enough to be argued as expanding the commission's operative powers under Article 3. A court could be asked whether the finding controls or merely explains the operative sections.

The declaration that the compact provides for "a joint exercise of such powers of sovereignty" is a finding that parties invoke against the operative reservations of state authority in Sections 5.5, 11.1(c) and 11.2(c). Whether the finding qualifies those savings clauses is a question of construction.

The finding that "a single administrative agency is therefore essential" sits against Section 1.5, which directs preservation and use of existing offices and agencies, and against the savings clauses in Sections 5.5, 11.1(c) and 11.2(c). Which prevails when the commission and a state agency both claim a subject is left open.

The finding that the basin's waters "are ample to meet all presently projected demands" cannot be squared with Sections 10.2 and 10.4, which presuppose water shortages, protected areas and supply emergencies. A party could argue the finding limits the shortage powers, or that the finding is spent.

The declared purpose "to make secure and protect present developments within the states" pulls against the operative approval requirement in Section 3.8 and the withdrawal controls in Article 10, which can defeat existing developments. Which reading of the compact's purpose governs interpretation of those operative powers is contestable.

Section 1.4's saving of congressional powers is qualified in Part II by Section 15.1(b) and 15.1(s), which are themselves expressed as "applicable to the extent not inconsistent with Section 1.4." The circular cross-reference leaves it unclear which text yields when they conflict.

Section 1.5's direction to preserve existing agencies "to the extent not inconsistent with the compact" cannot be squared straightforwardly with Section 1.3(c)'s declaration that a single administrative agency is essential. The phrase "to the fullest extent it finds feasible and advantageous" also leaves the duty entirely to the commission's own judgment.

The renewal condition — continuation "if not later than 20 years nor sooner than 25 years prior to the termination" none of the signatory states gives notice — combines an inverted time window with a double negative, and is readily read two ways. It also speaks only of "signatory states," leaving the federal signatory's power to terminate unaddressed.

Paragraph (b) speaks of termination "by operation of paragraph (a)," but paragraph (a) operates to continue the compact; termination results from state notice, not from the paragraph. The winding-up is also left "in such manner as may be provided by act of the Congress," with no fallback if Congress does not act.

Calling the commission "an agency and instrumentality of the governments of the respective signatory parties" cannot be squared with Section 15.1(m), which provides that for the enumerated federal statutes the commission "shall not be considered a Federal agency." The commission's status for immunity and procedural purposes therefore turns on which provision governs.

Section 2.2 provides that the federal commissioner serves "during the term of office of the President," while Section 15.1(d) provides that he "shall serve at the pleasure of the President." The two cannot both be given effect on tenure, as the compact's own endnote acknowledges.

The rule that an alternate "shall serve during the term of the member appointing him, subject to removal at the pleasure of the member" conflicts with Section 15.1(d), which makes the federal alternate serve at the pleasure of the President rather than of the member. The saving phrase "unless otherwise provided by law of the signatory party" may or may not absorb that.

Section 2.4 says members and alternates "shall serve without compensation," while Section 15.1(r) provides that, "the provisions of Sections 2.4 and 2.6 ... notwithstanding," the federal member and alternate may be paid by the United States. The two provisions state opposite rules for the same officers.

"A majority of the membership" does not say whether it means a majority of the full membership or of those present and voting, and Section 14.5(a) uses the contrasting phrase "majority of the full membership." The difference decides whether business can be done with absent members.

Section 2.6 leaves the appointment of an advisor to "each member in his discretion," but New York's § 632(1) mandates that its member's advisor "shall be the mayor of the city of New York or his designee." The state enactment and the compact provision cannot both be given full effect.

The commission may act outside the basin "whenever such action may be necessary or convenient to effectuate its powers or duties within the basin," a standard with no articulated limit and set entirely by the commission's own discretion. "Convenient" in particular carries no measurable boundary.

Section 3.2(b) requires a water resources program covering "such reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine," while Section 13.1's counterpart, Section 13.2, fixes "the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period." Because 3.2 is expressly to be exercised "in accordance with Article 13," the two statements of the program's period must be reconciled.

The grant to allocate waters "in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment" is hard to square with Section 3.3(b), which says no such action "shall be deemed to constitute an apportionment of the waters of the basin among the parties." What the commission is doing when it allocates, and with what legal effect, comes out only when the two are read together.

The paragraph uses two different unanimity requirements — "unanimous consent of the parties to the ... decree" and "unanimous consent of its members" — in successive clauses governing overlapping subject matter. Which consent is required for a given emergency action, and for how long "such limited time" runs, is left uncertain.

Paragraph (b)'s statement that no allocation constitutes an apportionment cannot be squared with the opening of Section 3.3, which directs the commission to allocate "in accordance with the doctrine of equitable apportionment." A court would have to decide whether allocations create enforceable entitlements at all.

"Any proper party deeming itself aggrieved" is undefined, and the section gives no test of who qualifies for de novo Supreme Court review as against ordinary judicial review "in any court of competent jurisdiction." The line between an "out-of-basin diversion" action and "any other action of the commission" is equally unmarked.

The waiver is followed by an exception permitting proceedings "to increase diversions or compensating releases in connection with such increased diversions" but not decreases, though the waiver itself covers both. Whether that asymmetry is deliberate or a drafting slip governs what modifications remain available.

Section 3.5's flat prohibitions on impeding the decree sit against Section 3.3(a), which lets the commission by unanimous vote increase or decrease decree diversions and releases in an emergency. The opening "except as specifically provided in Sections 3.3 and 3.4" is the only bridge, and its scope is contestable.

Paragraph (h) is a general catch-all — "such other and different powers ... and ... all powers necessary or convenient to carry out its express powers or which may be reasonably implied therefrom" — appended to seven enumerated specifics. Whether it expands the commission's authority beyond the enumeration or is confined by it is a classic ejusdem generis dispute.

Section 3.7's grant of rate-setting power "without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party" is directly cut back by Section 15.1(b), which forbids charges for withdrawals lawfully free at the effective date and for commercial navigation. The two cannot both be given full effect as written.

"No project having a substantial effect on the water resources of the basin" turns approval jurisdiction on an undefined threshold — "substantial effect" — with no measure supplied here or in Article 13. The same is true of the approval test, "substantially impair or conflict with the comprehensive plan."

Section 3.8 subjects projects undertaken "by any person, corporation or governmental authority" to review, but Section 1.2(g) defines "project" by reference to work "separately planned, financed, or identified by the commission." Whether private undertakings the commission never identified are within Section 3.8 is only resolvable by reading the two together.

The introductory clause reads "To this end, but with limitation thereto, the commission may," where the parallel provisions (Sections 3.5, 4.1 and 3.6(b)) read "without limitation thereto." The apparent omission of "out" reverses the sense of the sentence, making the enumerated powers exhaustive rather than illustrative.

Section 4.1's grant of power to build and operate water supply works "without limitation thereto" runs up against Section 4.5's proviso that nothing authorizes the commission "to engage in the business of distributing water." Where supply ends and distribution begins is settled only by reading the two together.

The enumerated purposes for storage and release close with "and other purposes," a catch-all with no limiting principle after a list of water-quality and public-benefit purposes. Its reach against the specific enumeration is contestable.

The prohibition on permitting augmentation of flow to be diminished by diversion excepts diversions "duly authorized by this compact," which must be read against Sections 3.3(a) and 3.5, protecting decree diversions from commission interference. Whether decree diversions are within the exception or beyond the prohibition altogether is left unclear.

Assessments may be laid on water users "specially benefited thereby to a measurable extent," and "no such assessment shall exceed the actual benefit to any water user" — two benefit standards with no method of measurement stated. Whether "actual benefit" is measured as in Section 1.2(d)'s definition of cost is not said.

Section 4.4 requires a public hearing "on each proposed project" under Article 4, while Section 14.4(b) enumerates the occasions on which hearings are required and adds "all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing." Whether the ten-day notice regime of 14.4(b) governs each Article 4 project hearing must be worked out between them.

"The business of distributing water" is not defined, and the same sentence grants power to provide "transmission facilities," which may amount to distribution. The boundary between an authorized transmission facility and a forbidden distribution business is unmarked.

The pollution standard — that waste "shall not injuriously affect waters of the basin as contemplated by the comprehensive plan" — has no stated threshold and is anchored to a plan the commission itself writes under Section 13.1. "Injuriously affect" carries no measurable boundary.

The covenant to "enact any necessary legislation" and to keep waters "in a satisfactory condition" describes the required condition only by open-ended adjectives — "safe and satisfactory," "suitable," "free from unsightly or malodorous nuisances." What performance would discharge a signatory's covenant cannot be determined from the words.

Enforcement orders are made "reviewable in any court of competent jurisdiction," a phrase New York's § 634 redefines for its courts and Section 15.1(p) overlays with exclusive-sounding federal district court original jurisdiction. Where review of a cease order lies is resolved only by reading the three together.

Section 5.5's saving of each state's power to "enforce any additional conditions and restrictions" against pollution is hard to square with Section 5.2, under which the commission "may assume jurisdiction" to control pollution, and with Section 10.8's supersession rule. Whether a stricter state rule survives commission occupation of the field is the point of tension.

The commission may adopt only "recommended standards" for flood plain land use, yet Section 6.3 requires its own flood land acquisitions to be "in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2." Whether standards that are merely recommended can have binding effect is left unresolved.

Paragraph (b) allows the commission to "establish encroachment lines" and standards for flood plain use, which reads as regulatory, while paragraph (a) confines its power to "recommended standards" that cannot restrict state or local zoning. The two paragraphs describe different legal effects for the same standards.

Section 6.3 requires acquisitions to be "in accord with the standards adopted and promulgated pursuant to Section 6.2," but Section 6.2(a) authorizes only "recommended standards" that expressly do not restrict local land use power. The condition on the acquisition power thus points to a source that may have no binding content.

The commission may not operate a project unless it finds "no other suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions" — neither "suitable" nor "reasonable conditions" is given content. The bar to the commission's own operation is therefore unmeasurable.

Section 8.1 directs that the commission "shall provide for the development" of recreational facilities and may construct and administer them, but makes this "subject to ... Section 8.2," which forbids it to operate any such facility where another government unit is available. The mandatory duty and the operating bar have to be reconciled.

The operating bar turns on whether another "suitable unit or agency of government is available to operate the same upon reasonable conditions," terms that are undefined and left to the commission's own finding. No benchmark of suitability or reasonableness is supplied anywhere in Article 8.

The duties are imposed "within limits prescribed by this article," but Article 8 prescribes no express limits other than the Section 8.2(b) operating bar and the Section 8.4 bidding requirement. What the phrase restricts is indeterminate.

Section 8.4 mandates competitive sealed bidding for all private concessions, but Section 15.1(l) provides that Section 8.4 "shall not be construed to apply to facilities operated pursuant to any other Federal law." Which concessions escape the bidding requirement depends on reading the two together.

"The business of direct sale to consumers" is not defined, and the same sentence authorizes transmission facilities "for the purpose of wholesale marketing of power." The line between prohibited direct sale and permitted wholesale marketing is unmarked.

Development contracts must be on "reasonable terms, consideration and duration," a standard with no benchmark and no cross-reference to the rate standards of Section 9.5. Reasonableness of consideration in particular has no stated measure.

Power rates must be "reasonable, nondiscriminatory, and just," but Section 3.7 lets the commission fix rates "without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party." Who tests the rates against that standard, and by what measure, is not stated.

Section 10.1 lets the commission delegate its regulatory powers to signatory parties, while New York's § 637 forbids any of its agencies to accept a delegation it could not exercise on its own account absent the compact. The delegation power and the state enactment do not sit comfortably together.

A protected area may be declared where demands "have developed or threaten to develop to such a degree as to create a water shortage," with no definition of shortage or of the degree of threat required. "Threaten to develop" gives the designation power no measurable trigger.

The permit requirement excepts withdrawals "pursuant to a permit or approval heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states," but Section 10.8 provides that state-issued diversion and withdrawal permits are superseded to the extent of any conflict with commission regulation. The grandfather clause and the supersession clause cannot both be given full effect.

The emergency provision bars any entity from withdrawing water "for any purpose" in excess of prescribed quantities, without the grandfather exception that Section 10.3 gives to pre-existing state permits and without regard to Sections 3.3(a) and 3.5's protection of decree diversions. Whether decree and pre-existing rights survive an emergency declaration is unaddressed.

Permits turn on avoiding depletion that "will adversely affect the comprehensive plan or the just and equitable interests and rights of other lawful users," while "giving due regard to the need to balance and reconcile alternative and conflicting uses." The standard names competing considerations without any rule of priority among them.

Judicial review is expressly given for determinations under Section 10.2 and permits under Sections 10.3 through 10.5, and for nothing else in Article 10 — inviting an expressio unius argument that actions under Sections 10.7 and 10.8 are unreviewable. The enumeration's exclusivity is the contestable point.

Section 10.8 supersedes state-issued diversion and withdrawal permits "to the extent of any conflict," while Section 10.3(ii) preserves withdrawals made under permits "heretofore granted under the laws of any of the signatory states." The two provisions give opposite answers on pre-existing state permits.

The consultation duty attaches to "all projects related to powers delegated to the commission by this compact," a class defined by an undefined relation to a broad set of delegated powers. What relation suffices is not stated.

Paragraph (b) forbids any federal expenditure or commitment for a project not first included in the comprehensive plan and says it shall not "be deemed authorized," which cannot be squared with paragraph (c)'s preservation of each federal agency's existing authority or with Section 15.1(s)(1)'s preservation of federal powers. The scope of the bar is only intelligible once those provisions are read against it.

Paragraph (c) preserves each federal agency's authority to plan, construct and operate projects "except as specifically provided by this section," while paragraph (b) bars any expenditure on a project not in the comprehensive plan. Whether (b) is such a specific provision, swallowing (c), is the question.

The consultation duty covers "all projects related to powers delegated to the commission by this compact," with no test of relatedness and with "project" carrying the contested Section 1.2(g) definition. Which state and local undertakings are caught is therefore indeterminate.

Paragraph (b) bars any state or local expenditure on a project not first included in the comprehensive plan, while paragraph (c) preserves each state and local agency's existing authority to construct and operate projects. The two paragraphs of the same section pull in opposite directions.

Paragraph (c) preserves state and local agency authority "except as specifically provided by this section," but paragraph (b) forbids the expenditures by which that authority would be exercised. Which is the rule and which the exception cannot be told from the section alone.

The states' reserved right to levy fees and taxes "measured by the withdrawal or diversion of waters" sits against Section 3.5(b), which forbids any fee or charge on decree-permitted diversions, and Section 3.7, which lets the commission fix charges free of state control. Whose exaction survives on the same withdrawal is not settled.

The commission must develop "equitable cost sharing and reimbursement formulas," with equity as the only criterion and no method of determination supplied. The enumerated subparagraphs describe machinery, not the standard.

Section 11.5 has each signatory party "pledge itself to provide technical and administrative services to the commission upon request," but Section 15.1(h) provides that, notwithstanding Section 11.5, federal agencies are pledged only so far as they agree or the President directs. The pledge and the reservation state contradictory obligations for the United States.

The section says bonds "shall be payable solely out of the properties and revenues of the commission without recourse to taxation" and in the next sentence that they "shall be direct and general obligations of the commission" backed by its full faith and credit. The limited-recourse and general-obligation characterizations are in tension.

The sentence reads "The purpose of this compact shall include without limitation thereto all costs of any project or facility," which conflates the compact's purposes with the purposes for which bonds may be issued and borrowed money spent. As written it appears to enlarge Section 1.3's purposes rather than define permitted bond expenditures.

Section 12.3 denies the commission any power to pledge a signatory party's credit or impose bond payment obligations on it, while Section 12.20(b) contemplates bonds sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party." Whether a signatory guaranty is permissible turns on reconciling the two.

The indenture may contain any covenants "other than any restriction on the regulatory powers vested in the commission by this compact," yet the enumerated permissible covenants include covenants as to "the rates or amounts of fees, rents and other charges," which Section 3.7 makes a regulatory power. The exclusion and the enumeration overlap.

"No bond or its terms shall mature in more than fifty years from its own date" is ungrammatical — terms do not mature — and it is unclear whether the fifty-year cap limits final maturity only or every payment obligation under the bond.

Section 12.8 exempts commission bonds and their interest from "all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties," but Section 15.1(f) preserves federal internal revenue taxation of those same bonds except to the extent state bonds are exempt. Since the United States is a signatory party, the two provisions conflict on their face.

Section 12.9 lets the commission set the interest rate without limit, while Section 12.13 caps the net interest cost of a below-par issue at six percent per annum. Whether the 1984 amendment to 12.9 displaced that cap is a question the two sections raise together.

Section 12.13 requires that "all bonds issued and sold for cash pursuant to this act shall be sold on sealed proposals to the highest bidder," while Section 12.20(b) permits delivery to a signatory agency "without public offering" notwithstanding any other provision. The mandatory bidding rule and the exemption must be reconciled.

A validation judgment is declared "conclusive against all persons whomsoever and against each of the signatory parties," without any provision for notice or participation by those bound. Whether the in rem proceeding can bind absent parties as stated is contestable on the face of the words.

The revenues are made a "first, direct and exclusive charge and lien" for bondholders, and in the same sentence may be applied to administration, operation, maintenance, improvements, extensions "or other purposes" as the indenture provides. The exclusivity of the lien and the open-ended exception cannot both be taken at face value.

The signatory parties "will provide such capital funds required for projects," yet the same sentence says nothing in the section "shall be deemed to impose any mandatory obligation on any of the signatory parties." The promise and the disclaimer sit in a single sentence and cancel each other.

Paragraph (b) permits bonds to be sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party," while Section 12.3 denies the commission power to impose any obligation for payment of the bonds upon a signatory party. Whether a guaranty may be given, and by whom, requires reading the two together.

The comprehensive plan "shall include all public and private projects and facilities which are required, in the judgment of the commission," so its content depends entirely on the contested Section 1.2(g) definition of "project" and feeds directly into the Section 3.8 approval test. Whether private undertakings must appear in the plan at all is settled only by reading the three provisions together.

Section 13.2 requires an annual program covering "the ensuing six years or such other reasonably foreseeable period as the commission may determine," while Section 3.2(b) states the same duty without the six-year benchmark. The governing period, and whether the commission may vary it at will, comes out only from the pair.

The balancing apportionment among signatory parties must be made "by unanimous vote of the commission," while Section 2.5 provides that no action is taken unless a majority votes in favor and gives each member one vote. The two voting rules for the same body must be reconciled, and nothing says what happens if unanimity fails.

The signatory parties "covenant and agree to include the amounts so apportioned" in their budgets, but only "subject to such review and approval as may be required by their respective budgetary processes." The qualification may leave the covenant with no enforceable content.

Subparagraph 6) confers "all corporate powers essential to the declared objects and purposes of the commission," a catch-all appended to five enumerated auxiliary powers. Whether it adds anything beyond the enumeration, and what "essential" measures, is contestable.

The hearing and filing requirements apply to every rule "other than one which deals solely with the internal management of the commission," a category that is nowhere defined and that the commission itself would classify. Rules of mixed character fall on neither side of the line.

The in-lieu payment clause is ambiguous in its grammar: "annual amounts which shall equal the taxes lawfully assessed ... for the tax year next prior to its acquisition by the commission for a period of ten years" leaves unclear whether the ten years qualifies the payment obligation or the measuring tax year. The following sentence's review "at the end of ten years" assumes the former without saying so.

"All meetings of the commission shall be open to the public" admits of no exception, yet Section 14.2(a) contemplates rules dealing "solely with the internal management of the commission" and Section 14.5(a) contemplates personnel decisions. Whether any deliberation may be closed is unaddressed.

The section requires hearings "in all other cases wherein this compact requires a public hearing," while Section 4.4 independently requires a hearing on each proposed Article 4 project and Section 3.7 requires "public notice and hearing." Whether the ten-day posted-notice regime governs all of those is only answerable across the provisions.

The executive director is appointed and removable "by the affirmative vote of a majority of the full membership," while Section 2.5 requires only that "a majority of the membership" vote in favor of any commission action. The deliberate difference in wording raises the question whether two different quorums operate.

"Financially interested, either directly or indirectly, in any contract, sale, purchase, lease or transfer" has no de minimis threshold or definition of indirect interest, though the commissioners are sitting Governors whose states contract with the commission. What counts as a disqualifying indirect interest is unmarked.

The forfeiture sanction reaches only "any officer or employee," although Section 14.8(a) imposes the prohibitions on "no commissioner, officer or employee." The omission of commissioners invites an expressio unius reading that they are subject to the prohibition but not the sanction.

"Any contract or agreement knowingly made in contravention of this section is void" does not say whose knowledge counts — the commissioner's, the commission's or the counterparty's. The consequences for an innocent third party contractor are therefore unsettled.

Contracts must be let to "the lowest responsible bidder," a term nowhere defined, and the five listed grounds for waiving competitive bids close with "services ... of a specialized or professional nature" rather than a general catch-all. Both the responsibility standard and the exclusivity of the waiver list are open to argument.
The audit must be made "as soon as practical after the closing of the fiscal year," a deadline with no outer limit and no consequence for delay. Nothing else in Article 14 supplies a date.

Each signatory's unrestricted right to examine "all" books and property "at any time" sits against Section 15.1(m), which withholds federal agency status from the commission, and against Section 14.11(c)'s separate GAO audit regime. Which access rights govern federal examiners is not stated in one place.

Subjecting the commission's financial transactions to audit by the General Accounting Office under the Comptroller General's rules is hard to square with Section 15.1(m)'s provision that the commission "shall not be considered a Federal agency," and with Section 2.1's characterization of it as an instrumentality of all signatory parties. The extent of federal audit control depends on reconciling them.

The clause reads "refuse to give all require assistance," an evident grammatical error for "all required assistance," leaving the scope of the duty whose breach forfeits office uncertain. It also makes forfeiture automatic without any finding procedure, unlike Section 14.5(b).

Loans from a signatory party "shall be repaid by the commission through the issuance of bonds or out of other income," while Section 12.1 makes all bonds payable solely from commission properties and revenues and Section 12.3 bars imposing bond obligations on signatory parties. The repayment promise's security must be read against those limits.

The condemnation power excludes "property of a signatory party and any property held, constructed, operated or maintained in connection with a diversion authorized by a United States Supreme Court decree," but the sentence's structure leaves unclear whether the second exclusion is qualified by the first or stands alone. The scope of the decree-related exclusion is the operative uncertainty.

Political subdivisions are "authorized and empowered ... to grant and convey to the commission, upon the commission's request," leaving it unclear whether the conveyance is permissive or compelled by the request. The words carry both readings.

The commission's share of relocation cost "shall not in any event exceed the expenditure required to serve the public convenience and necessity," a cap with no method of computation and using a term of art borrowed from utility regulation. Who determines that amount is not stated.

The blanket permission to occupy streets and highways is made "subject to such reasonable conditions as the highway department of the signatory party may require," with no standard of reasonableness and no mechanism for resolving a dispute. The grant and the state veto are stated together without priority.

The default penalty applies only "in the absence of such provision" by a signatory state's statute, leaving unclear whether a state statute covering some violations displaces the default for all, and whether a state penalty smaller than $50 ousts the range. "Attempts or conspires to violate any provision of this compact" is also undefined as to the mental element.

Tort liability is measured by the law applicable to "officers, agents and employees of the government of the United States," yet Section 15.1(m) provides that the commission is not to be considered a Federal agency for the purposes of the Federal Tort Claims Act statutes it cites. The two provisions point to opposite results on the commission's tort exposure and procedure.

The disclaimer that nothing affects state riparian rights law is difficult to square with Section 3.3's power to allocate the waters of the basin and Article 10's power to condition or deny withdrawals, both of which necessarily bear on riparian entitlements. Section 14.14(a) likewise authorizes condemnation of "riparian rights."

Amendments require "legislative action of any of the signatory parties concurred in by all of the others," while Section 15.1(q) reserves to Congress the unilateral "right to alter, amend, or repeal this Act" and Section 1.4 recognizes a federal power of unilateral modification. Whether the compact can be changed without unanimity turns on which provision governs.

Section 14.21 provides that invalidity of any provision leaves the remainder unaffected, but Section 15.1(t) provides that if Section 1.4 is held invalid the United States ceases to be a party and bound. The general severability rule and the specific consequence cannot both operate on the same event.

The compact becomes effective "thirty days after the enactment of concurring legislation" by all five parties, while the enacting acts of the United States (Section 15.3), Delaware (§ 1013), New Jersey (15.3), New York (§ 3) and Pennsylvania (Section 4) each state that they "take effect immediately." The date on which obligations attached requires reconciling the two.

The bar on undertaking "any project (as defined in such compact) ... beyond the planning stage" without an Act of Congress cannot be squared as written with Sections 3.6, 4.1 and 13.1, which authorize the commission to construct and operate projects on its own initiative. The carve-out for projects using "State supplied funds only" makes the boundary depend on funding rather than subject matter.

The paragraph forbids the commission to "impose any change for water withdrawals or diversions," where "change" is plainly an error for "charge." The mistake goes to the operative verb of the prohibition.

The reservation cuts back Section 3.7, which grants rate and charge power "without regulation or control by any department, office or agency of any signatory party," yet is itself made applicable only "to the extent not inconsistent with Section 1.4." Which of the three provisions governs a particular charge cannot be told from any one of them.

"The executive powers of the President in the event of a national emergency" are neither defined nor tied to any declaration mechanism, and the paragraph does not say which compact obligations yield to them. Its relation to the commission's own emergency powers in Sections 3.3(a) and 10.4 is unstated.

This reservation provides that the federal member and alternate "shall serve at the pleasure of the President," which contradicts Section 2.2's provision that the commissioner serves "during the term of office of the President." The compact's own endnote records that the two were inconsistent until Congress repealed this paragraph in 1997.

The sentence — "construed as impairing or in any manner affecting the applicability to all Federal funds budgeted and appropriated for use by the commission, or such authority over budgetary and appropriation matters as the President and Congress may have" — omits the object of "the applicability," leaving the saving clause without a stated subject. What law is preserved has to be supplied by the reader.

This reservation preserves federal internal revenue taxation of commission bonds, while Section 12.8 declares those bonds exempt from "all taxation by or under authority of any of the signatory parties" — a class that includes the United States. The two provisions give contradictory answers on federal taxation of the bonds.

The disclaimer of any United States obligation on commission bonds sits against Section 12.20(b), which contemplates bonds delivered to "any duly authorized agency of any of the signatory parties" and sold "with or without the guaranty of such signatory party." Whether a federal agency guaranty is possible depends on reading the two together.

This reservation makes federal technical services discretionary, expressly "notwithstanding the provisions of Section 11.5," under which each signatory party "pledges itself to provide technical and administrative services to the commission upon request." The pledge and the reservation state opposite obligations for the same party.

The Davis-Bacon requirement extends to works "undertaken by the commission or ... financially assisted by it," without saying what degree of assistance triggers it, and prescribes overtime for hours "in excess of eight hours in any workday or forty hours in any workweek, as the case may be." Neither the assistance threshold nor "as the case may be" has a determinate meaning.

The paragraph preserves other federal officers' water pollution functions and then provides that the exercise of those functions "shall not limit the authority of the commission to control, prevent, or abate water pollution" — a circular pairing that does not say which yields in an actual clash. Read with Article 5, the priority between the commission and federal pollution authorities is unresolved.

"Facilities operated pursuant to any other Federal law" is undefined and could cover any facility touched by federal authorization, which would swallow Section 8.4's competitive bidding requirement for concessions. The breadth of the exemption is the contestable point.

The provision that the commission "shall not be considered a Federal agency" for the enumerated statutes cannot be squared with Section 14.18, which measures the commission's tort liability by the law applicable to United States officers and employees under those same statutes. The commission's amenability to tort claims falls between the two.

Commission officers and employees are denied federal status "for any purpose," except the United States member, alternate and advisors, whose compensation Section 15.1(r) and Section 2.4 treat inconsistently. Which body of employment law governs the excepted persons is not stated in either place.

The bar on enlarging "the authority of any Federal agency other than the commission to participate in or to provide funds for projects" is difficult to square with Section 11.1(c), which preserves each federal agency's existing project authority, and with Section 15.2(b)'s authorization of appropriations and detailed personnel. What counts as enlargement is unmarked.

The grant of "original jurisdiction of all cases or controversies arising under the Compact" to the United States district courts sits against Section 3.3(c), which sends out-of-basin diversion disputes to the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction, and against the compact's repeated references to "any court of competent jurisdiction" as redefined by New York's § 634. Whether federal jurisdiction is exclusive can be answered only across these provisions.

Congress's reserved "right to alter, amend, or repeal this Act" cannot be squared with Section 14.20, which requires that amendments be adopted by one signatory party and "concurred in by all of the others." Whether the compact can be changed unilaterally by one party is the question the pair raises.

This paragraph permits compensation to the federal member, alternate and advisor "the provisions of Sections 2.4 and 2.6 ... notwithstanding," while Section 2.4 states that members and alternates "shall serve without compensation" and Section 2.6 that advisors serve without compensation. The two provisions state opposite rules and are reconciled only by the notwithstanding clause's reach.

The requirement that federal agencies "not substantially conflict" with the comprehensive plan, coupled with the President's power to "suspend, modify or delete any provision of the comprehensive plan," has to be squared with Sections 3.8 and 11.1(b), which condition all projects on inclusion in that plan. Which text controls a federal project not in the plan is unresolved, and "substantially conflict" has no stated measure.

Withdrawal of concurrence is permitted "at any time between the first and sixtieth day of the sixth year after the initial adoption of the comprehensive plan and of every sixth year thereafter," a formula that does not say how the six-year cycles are counted or how withdrawal interacts with concurrences in later revisions. The presumption of concurrence after 60 days compounds the uncertainty.

This paragraph makes invalidity of Section 1.4 end the United States' participation, which cannot be squared with Section 14.21's severability rule that invalidity of any provision leaves the remainder and its applicability to other parties unaffected. The two provisions prescribe different consequences for the same event.

"All Acts or parts of Acts inconsistent with the provisions of this Act are hereby amended" identifies no statute and no measure of inconsistency, and the proviso that no act of the commission may repeal or amend federal law pulls in the other direction. What has been amended, and by how much, cannot be told from the words.

"This Act shall take effect immediately" cannot be squared with Section 14.22, under which the compact becomes binding only thirty days after concurring legislation by all five parties. The heading's own text ("Effect Date") is also garbled.

The repealer strikes "all acts and parts of acts inconsistent with any provision of this act" without identifying any statute or any test of inconsistency. What Delaware law survives is left to later litigation.

Delaware's act takes effect "immediately," while Section 14.22 postpones the compact's binding effect to thirty days after all five parties have enacted concurring legislation. The date from which Delaware was bound depends on reconciling the two.

New Jersey's repealer is numbered "15.1," the same designation as the United States' Section 15.1 Reservations in the same Part II, so a cross-reference to "Section 15.1" is ambiguous as between two entirely different provisions. The repealer's own scope — "all acts and parts of acts inconsistent" — is also left undefined.

The New Jersey act takes effect "immediately," while Section 14.22 makes the compact binding only thirty days after concurring legislation by all five parties. The two dates cannot both govern New Jersey's obligations.

The last sentence provides that in the absence of the governor and his alternate the powers shall be performed by "the alternate of said department head on the water resources commission," though no department head has been identified anywhere in the section. The chain of substitution therefore has no ascertainable referent.

New York directs that expenses be reimbursed "from the funds of said person's department or office," while Section 2.4 provides that members and alternates "may be reimbursed" by the commission for necessary expenses. Which body bears the cost is answered differently by the two provisions.

New York fixes its member's advisor as "the mayor of the city of New York or his designee," while Section 2.6 leaves the appointment of an advisor to "each member in his discretion." The state command and the compact's discretionary rule cannot both be given full effect.

This section conditions New York's consent under "subdivision three of section three of article three of the compact" — Section 3.3(a) — on prior approval of the state water resources commission, though Section 3.3(a) speaks of the unanimous consent of the parties to the decree and of the commission's own members. Whether an internal state precondition can qualify the compact's consent mechanism is contestable.

The exclusion of "section four hundred fifty-two of the conservation law" is drawn by reference to "diversions governed by subdivision one of this section," a class defined only by that cross-reference. Which diversions remain subject to state law is therefore hard to identify from the text.

New York defines "court of competent jurisdiction" as used throughout the compact to mean its own supreme court, while Section 15.1(p) gives the United States district courts original jurisdiction of all cases arising under the compact and makes state-court cases removable. The state definition and the federal reservation cannot both govern the same suit.

New York bars any state license for a project that "requires approval of the Delaware River Basin Commission pursuant to the compact," a class defined by Section 3.8's undefined "substantial effect" test and Section 1.2(g)'s contested definition of "project." Which projects the bar catches cannot be determined without construing those provisions.

New York forbids its agencies to accept any delegation under Section 10.1 unless they would have the power absent the compact, while Section 10.1 authorizes the commission to delegate "such powers of the commission as it may deem necessary or desirable." The delegation power and the state restriction are in tension.

New York requires the commission to submit its funding estimate to the state budget director "for study and consideration," while Section 13.3(b) has the apportionment among signatory parties fixed by unanimous vote of the commission and merely certified to each state. Whether the state's budget review can alter the apportioned amount is unresolved between them.

New York disapplies every state law "inconsistent with the provisions of the compact" to any matter governed by the compact, which is hard to square with Section 5.5's preservation of state power to impose additional pollution restrictions and Section 14.19's preservation of state riparian rights law. What state law survives depends on reconciling them.

The section makes the compact binding "in accordance with the provisions of subdivision twenty-one of section fourteen of article fourteen" and directs the governor to sign "as provided in said subdivision twenty-one," but Section 14.21 is Construction and Severability; the effective date and execution provisions are in Section 14.22. The cross-reference points to the wrong subdivision.

The New York act takes effect "immediately," while Section 14.22 delays the compact's binding effect until thirty days after all five parties have enacted concurring legislation. The two effective-date rules must be reconciled.

The repealer strikes "all acts and parts of acts inconsistent with any provision of this act" without naming a statute or supplying any test of inconsistency. What Pennsylvania law it displaces is left entirely open.

The Pennsylvania act takes effect "immediately," while Section 14.22 provides that the compact becomes binding thirty days after concurring legislation by all five parties. The date from which Pennsylvania was bound turns on which provision governs.
